READING 45
RELATIVE VALUE EQUITY
VALUATION APPROACHES
MODULE 45.1: PRICE MULTIPLES AND EQUITY
VALUATION
LOS 45.a: Explain the process for using multiples to value equity based on
the method of comparables and the method of forecasted fundamentals.
Relative valuation models compare the price or enterprise value of a security to
some metric of value. Price multiples divide the current market price of a stock
by its earnings per share, free cash flow to equity per share, or book value per
share. Enterprise value (EV) multiples divide the EV by EBITDA, free cash
flow to the firm, or revenue.
A multiple that uses a value from the past period in its denominator is called a
trailing multiple. One that uses a forecast value for the next period is called a
leading multiple or forward multiple. A justified multiple is an analyst’s
estimate of the multiple that a stock trading at its fair value should exhibit.
An analyst must choose the most appropriate multiple for any given valuation.
For example, when a company’s earnings are negative, its price-to-earnings ratio
is meaningless.
To determine whether a stock is fairly valued at its current price, analysts
compare the company’s multiples to a benchmark. When a price multiple is
higher than its benchmark value, the stock is considered overvalued; when a
price multiple is lower than its benchmark, the stock is seen as undervalued.
There are two approaches to defining a benchmark for a company: (1) the
method of comparables and (2) the method of forecasted fundamentals.
Method of Comparables

The method of comparables values a stock based on the average or median of
peer companies’ price multiples. The economic rationale for the method of
comparables is the “law of one price,” which implies that two similar assets
should be priced at similar multiples (e.g., P/E ratios).
The similar companies chosen as a benchmark are called a peer group. A valid
peer group must be truly comparable in terms of the included companies’
competitive positions, risk, and earnings growth rates. Variations in accounting
methods, nonrecurring items, and timing differences (due to fiscal year-end
reporting periods differing among companies) can make comparisons difficult.
While the average multiple of a firm’s peer group is commonly used as the
benchmark or justified multiple, if the distribution of the multiple is skewed, it
makes more sense to use the median multiple. Analysts may also remove outliers
from the peer group before calculating the mean.
Analysts must choose an appropriate multiple to use in a comparables-based
valuation. For example, a dividend-based multiple is inappropriate when the peer
group includes non-dividend-paying firms.
Method of Forecasted Fundamentals
The method of forecasted fundamentals determines the benchmark value
based on a discounted cash flow model. For example, we might start with a
constant growth model:
If we divide both sides by expected earnings per share for the next period (E1),
we arrive at a justified leading P/E ratio:
The leading P/E ratio indicates that the multiple is positively related to the
earnings growth rate and negatively related to the required rate of return (i.e., the
risk of the company).
We can also create a justified price-to-book value multiple based on this model.
First, we divide both sides by the firm’s book value of equity per share:

We can refine this multiple further by stating the expected dividend in the next
period (D1) as the product of the firm’s expected earnings per share and its
dividend payout ratio:
Then, because

relationship:
Next, recall that the relationship between ROE and the payout ratio gives us an
estimate of the firm’s sustainable growth rate (g). We can rearrange this
relationship:
g = ROE × (1 − dividend payout ratio)
g = ROE − (ROE × dividend payout ratio)
ROE × dividend payout ratio = ROE − g
Substituting this into the price-to-book-value relationship, we arrive at the
justified P/B ratio:
This relationship implies that the multiple depends on the difference between a
company’s actual ROE and its required rate of return on equity (or cost of
equity). A higher spread of ROE over r leads to a higher P/B multiple.
Reconciling the Methods
The method of comparables and method of forecasted fundamentals may yield
conflicting results that need reconciliation. For example, a firm’s justified P/E
ratio might be higher than the average of its peers, but that is acceptable when
the firm’s earnings growth rate is higher than those of its peers.
We can reconcile these approaches in two ways:

Modify the peer value based on the fundamental variable that causes the
difference, then compare the modified multiples. This approach only considers
one fundamental variable at a time.
The price/earnings-to-growth ratio (PEG) is commonly used to standardize
the P/E ratio based on firms’ expected growth rates:
The growth rate g in the PEG ratio is expressed as a percentage, rather than a
decimal.
The PEG ratio controls for growth rate differences across firms. If a firm has
a higher PEG ratio relative to peers, its P/E is higher than justified by its
growth rate, so its stock is overvalued.

rate forecast of 14.5%. The median PEG ratio for a group of companies
comparable in risk to Med-Ready is 2.34. Calculate the firm’s PEG ratio and
explain whether the stock appears to be correctly valued, overvalued, or
undervalued.

for one or more fundamental variables. The fundamental variables are the
independent (or X) variables, and the observed multiple is the dependent (or
Y) variable. Peer group data are used to estimate the regression coefficients.
Consider a model using the P/B ratio as the dependent variable, and ROE and

P/Bi = b0 + b1 × ROEi + b2 × g + ei
Using the peer group as the sample, estimates of b0, b1, and b2 are generated.
These estimates are then used to calculate the justified P/B ratio of the subject

Multiple regression is addressed in the Level II curriculum. The Level I
exam will not require you to perform or analyze a multiple regression,
but it might ask you to interpret the results of one, such as what we

Alpha, Inc.’s, ROE is 14%, its required rate of return is 8%, and its expected
growth rate is 4%. Rob Elwell uses a two-factor regression model using ROE
and g to analyze the P/B ratio of a peer group of 10 companies.
The estimated regression intercept is 1.42, the estimated coefficient for ROE is
6.78, and the estimated coefficient for the growth rate is 12.79.
Calculate and interpret a justified P/B ratio for Alpha, using both the method of
forecasted fundamentals and the regression method.

Justified P/B ratio = 1.42 + 6.78 × 0.14 + 12.79 × 0.04 = 2.88
Based on forecasted fundamentals, the stock should trade at 2.50 times book
value per share. Based on the regression model, the stock should trade at 2.88

Price multiples can also be used to determine a terminal value to use in present
value models. Analysts can estimate a justified price multiple at the end of the
forecast horizon, or when the growth rate stabilizes. Using the forecast
fundamental variables, an analyst can calculate a justified future price multiple
and use it to estimate the terminal value.
For example, a terminal value based on a justified P/E ratio is:

terminal value in year n = justified leading P/E ratio
                                        × forecast earnings in year (n + 1)

MODULE 45.2: PRICE AND ENTERPRISE VALUE
MULTIPLES
LOS 45.b: Calculate and interpret price and enterprise value multiples, and

A firm that earns a return above its required rate of return would benefit from
retaining earnings and investing in those growth opportunities, rather than
paying out dividends. Viewed this way, the value of its stock represents the
present value of its current dividend as a perpetuity (i.e., assuming no growth)
plus its present value of growth opportunities (PVGO):
This means the value of a firm’s equity has two components:
The value of its assets in place

cash flow of E1.

Core and Normalized Earnings
The P/E ratio is meaningless when earnings are negative, and it can be
unrepresentative of a stock’s value when earnings include substantial
nonrecurring items. Analysts typically try to estimate a company’s core
earnings (also called persistent earnings or continuing earnings). Core
earnings exclude nonrecurring components such as gains and losses from asset
sales, asset write-downs, provisions for future losses, changes in accounting
estimates, or income or losses from discontinued operations.
Earnings may also exhibit cyclicality, changing systematically over a business
cycle. Analysts adjust P/E ratios for cyclicality by estimating normalized
earnings, which estimate EPS in the middle of a business cycle. The following
two methods are used to normalize earnings:
Under the method of historical average EPS, normalized EPS is estimated as
the average EPS over the most recent business cycle.
Under the average ROE method, normalized EPS is estimated as average ROE
over the most recent business cycle times the current book value per share.
Using BVPS reflects the effect of changes in firm size more accurately than
does the method of historical average EPS.
EPS also needs to be adjusted to reflect the impact of dilution, changes in the
number of shares outstanding that result from exercise of employee stock
options, warrants, and convertible bonds.

Income Statement Measures
When earnings are negative or when differences in accounting methods make
earnings non-comparable across firms, analysts may use the price-to-sales (P/S)
multiple. The P/S multiple is suitable when comparing firms with similar
revenue recognition practices and for mature and cyclical firms.
We can calculate a justified P/S ratio 
 by multiplying a firm’s trailing P/E
ratio by its profit margin 
EXAMPLE: Calculating justified P/S ratio
A stock has a dividend payout ratio of 60%, an ROE of 8.3%, earnings per
share of $4.25, sales per share of $218.75, and an expected growth rate of 5%.
Shareholders require a return of 10% on their investment. Calculate a justified
P/S multiple based on these fundamentals.

Answer:
Sales revenue is available to both providers of debt and equity capital, while
price is an equity-only metric. For this reason, the P/S ratio is appropriate for
firms with little to no leverage. For more leveraged firms, it may be more
appropriate to use enterprise value in the numerator.
Other income statement measures include EBIT and EBITDA, which are
available to both shareholders and debtholders. Therefore, they are commonly
used in ratios with enterprise value (EV).
EV = market value of common and preferred stock + market value of debt − cash and short-term
investments
Alternatively, analysts may use firm value, which is the market value of a firm’s
equity and debt (the first two terms in EV).
Analysts also use free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) in EV ratios. Assuming a
constant growth rate:
Dividing both sides by EBITDA gives us the following expression for the
EV/EBITDA multiple:
EXAMPLE: EV/EBITDA multiple
Accel Industries has $100 million of EBITDA, $50 million of depreciation,
$60 million of capital expenditures, and $10 million of working capital

investment., Accel’s WACC is 7%, its tax rate is 20%, and its growth rate is
2%. Calculate Accel’s justified EV/EBITDA multiple.
Answer:
The EV/EBITDA ratio is often used for capital-intensive industries where
depreciation and amortization are large. EV/EBITDA is positively related to the
growth rate and negatively related to WACC.
Balance Sheet Measures
Book value of equity is commonly used in the P/B ratio. The P/B ratio is useful
for comparing firms with mostly tangible assets and similar accounting
practices, leverage, and asset profiles. For some industries, such as banks,
analysts use price-to-tangible book value, which excludes intangibles such as
goodwill from book value.
When peer firms have differences in financial leverage, or when book value is
negative, analysts may prefer to use the value-to-book multiple, which is firm
value divided by the book value of capital (i.e., book value of equity plus book
value of debt):
The enterprise value-to-book ratio uses EV in the numerator and removes cash
from the denominator:
We can also state an EV-to-book ratio in terms of the factors that drive it. Recall
the constant growth formula for EV:

Depreciation, capital expenditures, and working capital investment together
make up a firm’s reinvestment, the amount of its EBIT that is not available to
debtholders and equity holders. A firm’s reinvestment rate is its reinvestment as
a proportion of EBIT. We can state free cash flow to the firm in terms of the
reinvestment rate:
FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) × (1 − reinvestment rate)
We can define a firm’s return on capital (ROC) as the ratio of its after-tax
EBIT to its book value of capital:

algebra), we can express a ratio of EV-to-book value as follows:
EXAMPLE: EV-to-book value
Accel Industries has an EV / BV of capital ratio of 2.1x. Accel’s earnings are
growing at 3% and its WACC is 8%. Accel’s return on capital is 12% and its
reinvestment rate is 30%. Determine whether Accel is fairly valued,
overvalued, or undervalued.
Answer:
Because Accel’s current EV / BV of capital of 2.1 is greater than 1.68x, Accel
is overvalued.
Cash Flow Statement Measures
The price-to-dividend multiple is the ratio of a stock price to its dividends per
share. The dividend yield is the reciprocal of price-to-dividend multiple. A
trailing dividend yield is based on the dividend paid in the past year. A leading
dividend yield uses the expected dividend in the next year.

We can expand the dividend yield to express it as a function of the dividend
payout ratio and the firm’s earnings yield:

Inverting both sides of the equation gives us this expression for a justified

Unlike price multiples, with yield measures such as dividend yield or earnings
yield, a higher value than justified indicates an undervalued stock; a lower value
indicates an overvalued stock. As with multiples, yield measures are compared
to peers after controlling for differences in fundamental factors such as growth
rates and required ROE.
EXAMPLE: Justified dividend yield
Accel’s dividend payout ratio is 60%, while its justified trailing P/E multiple is
12. Betax’s required rate of return on equity is 10%, while its earnings have a
constant growth rate of 4%. Calculate Accel and Betax’s justified dividend
yield.
Answer:
Accel’s justified earnings yield is the reciprocal of its justified P/E, or 1/12.

While other cash flow statement items like CFO are also used in multiples,
FCFE is more appropriate because it more accurately reflects the cash available
to shareholders. Similarly, FCFF is appropriate to use for EV multiples because
it reflects cash available to both shareholders and debt holders.
Justified P/FCFE and EV/FCFF can be derived from their respective constant
growth models (after dividing both sides by the respective cash flow metric):
One concern with either free cash flow-based multiple is that these measures are
sensitive to fluctuations in capital expenditures and working capital investment,
which tend to be cyclical.
Analysts use unique price or EV multiples for some industries, based on
measures specific to those industries. For example, mining and oil firms may
have multiples based on production or developed reserves. A problem with this
approach is that these multiples are not comparable to other industries, which
can potentially lead to an entire industry becoming mispriced.

MODULE 45.3: PEER GROUPS AND MULTIPLES-
BASED VALUATION
LOS 45.c: Determine a potential peer group for multiples-based equity
valuation based on a company’s industry classification or specific drivers of
expected return.
Comparables-based valuation uses mean or median multiples of a peer group as
benchmarks. Peer groups can be determined based on (1) companies with the
same business activity as the subject company (an industry-based peer group) or
(2) companies with same statistical factor exposures to risk and return as the
subject company.
An industry-based peer group consists of firms with similar competitive forces,
supply chain dynamics, and technology. Analysts should still take care when
identifying peer group members because firms may have differences in their
fundamental factors (e.g., leverage) or exposure to multiple industries and
markets. Peers should be similar in terms of cyclicality, life cycle stage, and
market structure. The idea is that similar firms should generate similar cash
flows.
Issues analysts may encounter while using an industry-based peer group
include the following:
Unique firms with no (or few) similar companies
High variation among life cycle stages of the firms in an industry
Firms with exposure to different tax or regulatory jurisdictions
Multi-industry companies
Statistical factor-based peer groups comprise companies with the same or
similar risk-return factor exposures. While the CAPM is a single-factor model
that measures risk premium based on a company’s systematic risk (beta),
multifactor models (which we will discuss in a later reading) are more
commonly used in identifying a factor-based peer group. A disadvantage of this
approach is that statistical relationships based on past data might not persist
into the future, which can result in models being misspecified.

LOS 45.d: Describe the use of multiples based on past, current, and
projected future values in estimating equity value.
One concern with comparables-based valuation is that it fails to identify
overvalued or undervalued stocks when their peer companies are also overvalued
or undervalued. Another concern is that the multiples based on current values
(e.g., of earnings) may be influenced by accounting choices, nonrecurring items,
or cyclicality.
Alternatively, comparables may be based on two elements:
Historical values of the subject company’s multiples. This allows analysts to
recognize changes in the multiples over time and link them to changes in the
company’s fundamentals.
Historical averages of peer group multiples. This allows analysts to compare
the company’s multiples to its peers over time.
As mentioned earlier, multiples based on projected future values can be used to
estimate terminal values for present value models. In such a case, the forecast
multiple is applied to a forecast metric, such as earnings per share.

Level Partners is expected to have earnings in 10 years of $12 per share, a
dividend payout ratio of 30%, and a required return of 11%. At that time, the
dividend growth rate is expected to fall to 4% in perpetuity. Estimate the
terminal value at the end of 10 years.

1. Which of the following is least likely an issue with comparables valuation based on

A. Unique firms.

B. Multi-industry companies.
C. Similar life cycle stages of firms in an industry.
2. An analyst observes that Tiller Company’s P/E ratio is less than those of its industry

KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 45.a
The method of comparables values a stock based on the average or median price
multiple of its peer companies. The method of forecasted fundamentals estimates
the benchmark multiple based on a discounted cash flow model.
The PEG ratio controls for growth rate differences between comparable firms:
A regression approach can control for differences in multiple fundamentals.
Regression coefficients are estimated from a peer group sample.
LOS 45.b
A stock price theoretically represents the present value of a perpetuity of its
current dividend plus the present value of the company’s growth opportunities
(PVGO):
Core earnings exclude nonrecurring components. Normalized earnings are
estimated for the middle of the business cycle.
Normal EPS is calculated as the average EPS over the most recent business
cycle, or the average ROE over the cycle applied to the most recent book value
per share. Average ROE accounts for changes in firm size over time.
Compared to the price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple, a price-to-sales (P/S) multiple
is more suitable for mature, cyclical, and negative-earnings firms.

An EV/EBITDA multiple can be used for firms with different capital structures,
and for capital-intensive industries with significant depreciation and
amortization.
LOS 45.c
Peer groups can be identified as companies in the same industry (engaging in the
same principal activity), or as companies with the same statistical factor
exposures as the subject company.
Issues with industry-based peer group include unique firms, multi-industry
firms, variation in life cycle stages of companies in an industry, and firms in
different tax or regulatory jurisdictions.
LOS 45.d
Concerns for comparables-based valuation include that it can fail when the
comparables are mispriced, and that multiples are based on accounting data.
In addition to comparing multiples to peer companies, analysts can compare
multiples to their historical values for the subject company or to historical peer
averages.
